opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is that reinforcement learning works best when you have a reward signal that's cheap, fast, and unambiguous. If you're training a model to solve math problems or write code that passes unit tests, you can check the answer almost instantly, and that tight feedback loop is what lets RL scale. Research ideas don't have that property at all.

When you propose a research idea, the "reward" is something like: did this end up mattering? Did it open up a new direction, did people build on it, did it turn out to be true? That signal might take months or years to arrive, and it's incredibly noisy. Plenty of good ideas fail the first time because the execution was off, or the compute wasn't there yet, or the field wasn't ready. Neural networks themselves are the classic example. They were "bad ideas" for a long time until suddenly they weren't. So if you'd trained a verifier on the consensus at any given moment, it would have confidently told you to stop working on the thing that ended up mattering most.

There's also a taste component that's hard to articulate. Experienced researchers have intuitions about what's promising, but if you ask them to explain why, they often can't fully decompose it. It's built from years of seeing what worked and what didn't, and it's heavily context-dependent. That makes it hard to write down as a rubric, and if you try to learn it from human preference data, you risk just learning what sounds impressive rather than what's actually good. You end up optimizing for ideas that pitch well.

And then there's the credit assignment problem. Even if a project succeeds, was it the original idea, or the fifty small engineering decisions along the way? Research outcomes are so entangled with execution that isolating the quality of the idea itself is genuinely hard.

So to me, verification is the bottleneck. Generating lots of candidate ideas is relatively easy now. Language models can brainstorm all day. The hard part is knowing which one out of a thousand is worth spending six months on. Until we have some way to get a faster, more reliable proxy for that, whether through cheap small-scale experiments that predict large-scale results, or better simulation, RL on research itself is going to be operating with a very weak signal.

r001.rationale: It says research outcomes are entangled with execution and that isolating the idea’s quality is hard, identifying the difficulty of separating execution failure from a flawed idea.

r002.rationale: It notes that execution problems can make good ideas fail, but does not say that strong prior conviction leads a researcher to blame a failure on a bug.

r003.rationale: It describes ideas receiving weak or delayed signals, including neural networks being considered bad ideas for a long time before succeeding, as a challenge for RL.

r004.rationale: It suggests small-scale experiments or simulation as faster proxies, but does not pose the open question of how to design RL environments that give earlier feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that reinforcement learning works really well when you have a reward signal that's cheap, dense, and reliable. Games are the canonical example. You play Go, you win or you lose, and you can run millions of episodes. The verifier is essentially free.

Research is almost the opposite of that on every axis. The thing you're trying to verify is "was this a good idea?" and the only honest way to answer that is to actually go do the research. You have to run the experiments, wait for the results, sometimes wait months or years for the field to tell you whether it mattered. So the reward is incredibly sparse and incredibly expensive to compute. You can't just roll out a million trajectories and see what sticks.

And then there's the subtler problem, which is that a lot of what makes an idea good isn't visible at the moment of proposal. Some of the best ideas look dumb or obvious or wrong when you first hear them, and some of the worst ideas sound fantastic in a paper abstract. If you train a model to predict "does this sound like a good idea," you end up rewarding things that pattern-match to good ideas rather than things that actually are. That's a classic reward hacking setup. The model learns to write compelling proposals, not to be right.

So you have this gap between the proxy, which is "a smart person reads it and nods," and the ground truth, which is "it works and it changes something." Closing that gap means either making the ground truth cheaper, like building really fast experimental loops, or making the proxy much better, which basically requires taste. And taste is exactly the thing that's hard to formalize into a reward function. I think that's why I keep coming back to it as one of the central bottlenecks. If you could verify research ideas cheaply, a lot of the rest of automating science would follow pretty quickly.

r001.rationale: It describes research verification as expensive and delayed, but does not discuss distinguishing an implementation bug from a fundamentally flawed idea after failure.

r002.rationale: It does not say that strong prior conviction can lead a researcher to blame an experimental failure on a bug.

r003.rationale: It mentions long waits for results, but not a trajectory with discouraging intermediate feedback that eventually succeeds.

r004.rationale: It suggests faster experimental loops as one way to lower verification costs, but does not pose the open question of designing RL environments to give earlier feedback on research ideas.

astra-6.text:
The hard part is that coming up with an idea and knowing whether it’s good can be separated by a huge amount of work. You might have an idea for a new architecture, but to evaluate it you need to implement it, debug it, run experiments, and figure out whether a negative result means the idea is bad or you just got the implementation wrong.

For reinforcement learning, that makes the reward expensive, delayed, and noisy. In a game, you can play out a trajectory and get a clear win or loss. In research, an experiment failing doesn’t necessarily tell you which decision was wrong. Maybe the idea works at a different scale. Maybe it needs a different optimizer. Maybe you should abandon it—or maybe the breakthrough comes after another month of debugging.

So even if you can generate research ideas cheaply, you haven’t necessarily made the whole process cheap. You still need a way to distinguish promising ideas from plausible-sounding ones, and that verification can require doing much of the research itself.

r001.rationale: The response says a failed experiment may reflect an implementation error rather than a bad idea, and explains the difficulty of telling which.

r002.rationale: It mentions implementation error as one possible explanation for failure, but does not say that strong prior conviction leads a researcher to favor that explanation.

r003.rationale: It mentions that a breakthrough might come after more debugging, but does not describe discouraging intermediate feedback followed by eventual success as a long-horizon reinforcement learning problem.

r004.rationale: It does not pose the question of how to design reinforcement learning environments to provide earlier feedback on research ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, with reinforcement learning, you need some way to tell whether the thing you did was good. And research is tricky because the feedback is delayed, noisy, and often depends on what you do next. An idea might look bad because you haven’t found the right experiment yet, or it might produce a promising result that turns out to be an artifact.

You can verify narrower things, like whether a proof is correct or whether a model’s score improved. But that’s different from verifying whether the research direction was good. Did it teach you something important? Did it open up a useful line of work? Sometimes a failed experiment does that better than a successful one.

So the challenge is specifying a reward that captures scientific progress. If you reward whatever is easy to measure, you risk training a system to produce impressive-looking results rather than to discover things.

r001.rationale: The response says an idea may look bad before the right experiment is found, but it does not identify distinguishing an implementation bug from a fundamentally flawed idea.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss strong prior conviction leading a researcher to attribute failure to a bug.

r003.rationale: It mentions delayed, noisy feedback, but not research trajectories with discouraging intermediate feedback that eventually succeed as a long-horizon RL problem.

r004.rationale: It discusses specifying a reward for scientific progress, but does not pose the question of designing environments that provide earlier feedback on research ideas.
